extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (aesthetics), readers of Kant
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts Kant's criteria for making and assessing judgements of taste, including conditions for beauty and the sublime (normal Idea, Ideal, purposiveness, disinterestedness, common sense, mathematical vs dynamic sublime, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal Idea (average form / correctness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'normal Idea' is the image for the whole race that floats among the various intuitions of individuals and serves as the archetype of correctness for a species' form; it is not derived from fixed proportions of experience but is the basis that makes rules for judging possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant uses the example of averaging many images (a thousand men) to arrive at an 'average size'—the normal Idea pleases because it contradicts no condition under which a thing of that kind can be beautiful. It contains nothing specifically characteristic (otherwise it would not be normal). Examples: Doryphorus of Polycletus as rule; Myron's cow likewise. The normal Idea yields mere correctness in presentation rather than positive beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal (expression of the moral in the human figure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ideal (especially in the human figure) consists in the visible expression of the moral—goodness of heart, purity, strength, peace—which makes the object positively and universally pleasing beyond mere correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This Ideal requires a union of pure Ideas of Reason with great imaginative power to render inner moral ideas visible. A judgement according to such an Ideal is not a purely aesthetical judgement; it is not merely taste but involves moral Ideas and interest beyond purely aesthetic satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as purposiveness without representation of a purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is 'the form of the purposiveness of an object, so far as this is perceived in it without any representation of a purpose.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The key is that the object appears purposive (fits our cognitive faculties) although one does not represent any specific purpose for it. This is the central analytic definition tying aesthetic pleasure to 'purposiveness without purpose.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Free conformity to law of the Imagination (faculty of taste)
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste is the faculty for judging an object with reference to the Imagination's free conformity to law: the Imagination is considered productive and spontaneous, yet its product conforms to the Understanding's law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a judgement of taste the Imagination plays freely (not merely reproductive association) but still harmonizes with the Understanding. If Imagination is compelled by concepts, the satisfaction is in the Good (cognitive/perfect form) and not aesthetic taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemplary necessity / claim to universal assent
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement of taste presents a peculiar necessity: it claims that everyone 'ought' to give approval—i.e., it asserts an exemplary (subjective) necessity for universal assent that is not derived from concepts or empirical consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This necessity is not apodictic or practical but 'exemplary'—a demand for universal assent based on a subjective common ground. It cannot be grounded on definite concepts or mere experience, hence the judge appeals to a presupposed common sense ('sensus communis').

rubrics_metrics.name: Common sense (sensus communis) as the condition of necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste presupposes a 'common sense'—a subjective principle (distinct from common understanding) that determines what pleases by feeling yet with universal validity; this common sense is the condition for the universal communicability of aesthetic feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant argues we must presuppose a common sense so that feelings and cognitions admit of universal communicability; it is not empirical but a necessary subjective condition for making claims that others 'ought' to agree. The common sense is an ideal norm enabling the claim to universal assent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness (pleasure devoid of interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper judgement of taste is 'devoid of interest'—the pleasure taken in the beautiful is not founded on desire for the object's existence or on practical interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant distinguishes aesthetic pleasure from the pleasant (sensory) and the good (practical/cognitive). The aesthetic judgement's validity rests on feeling, not on concepts or interest; 'quality' of the judgement thereby requires disinterested pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposiveness without purpose (aesthetic purposiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic appreciation involves perceiving purposiveness in an object while not representing any determinate purpose—'purposiveness without purpose'—so that the Imagination and Understanding harmonize free of conceptual constraint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This notion explains why an object can be judged beautiful even when no practical function is apparent: the object's form appears as if designed for cognition, yet no specific purpose is posited. It underlies the 'free play' that characterizes taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of rigid mathematical regularity; valuing imaginative freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Stiff, mathematical regularity (constraint of rule) is repugnant to taste; pure taste prefers forms that permit free, unstudied play of the Imagination rather than forms determined solely by concept-driven regularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant notes that strictly regular geometrical figures may produce short-lived satisfaction tied to cognition, not taste. Examples: English garden taste or bizarre furniture pushing imagination near the grotesque; pepper-garden seen in a forest appeals because it contrasts with wild beauty. Repetition of strictly rule-based art (music) can weary the spectator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between aesthetic pleasure and purposive/cognitive satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Satisfaction derived from regularity when serving cognition or specific practical purposes (the Good) differs from aesthetic pleasure; where representation is determined by a concept, the approval is of the Good/perfection, not of the Beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular forms needed for intelligibility or use (e.g., rooms with right angles, symmetric buildings) please because they fit a purpose or cognitive design, not because they prompt free purposiveness of taste. Aesthetic judgement requires that Understanding not dominate Imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of the sublime: mathematically vs dynamically sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: The sublime divides into the mathematically sublime (relating to magnitude/quantity) and the dynamically sublime (relating to power affecting the faculty of desire); both are kinds of aesthetic reflective judgement but differ in how the Imagination is moved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant derives this division from whether the movement provoked by the sublime is referred to cognition (mathematical: limits of imagination in grasping magnitude) or to desire (dynamical: feeling of might/force). The method of analysing sublimity mirrors that of beauty but begins with quantity because the sublime often concerns boundlessness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical sublimity: 'absolutely great' and idea-based origin
rubrics_metrics.description: The mathematically sublime is 'absolutely great'—great beyond all comparison—and cannot be adequately represented by any sensible measure; its source is in Ideas of Reason rather than in sense-objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant asserts that nothing given to the senses can be strictly 'sublime' in itself; the sublime arises when imagination fails to comprehend magnitude fully, thereby arousing the Idea of the supersensible. Formula: 'the sublime is that in comparison with which everything else is small.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic estimation of magnitude: apprehension vs comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: In estimating magnitude aesthetically there are two operations: apprehension (which can extend ad infinitum) and comprehension (aesthetic comprehension reaches a maximum); when comprehension cannot keep up with apprehension, the feeling of the sublime arises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant explains that numeric/mathematical estimation differs from aesthetic estimation: the latter has a subjective maximum of comprehension. Practical illustration: to feel the full effect of the Pyramids' size, one must neither be too near nor too far—distance affects the balance of apprehension and comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime produces negative pleasure (admiration/respect) via a check and overflow of vital powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The sublime's pleasure is indirect and often negative: it arises from a momentary checking of the vital powers and a consequent stronger outflow, producing admiration or respect rather than charm or playful pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike the Beautiful, which supports a restful play of the Imagination, the Sublime alternately attracts and repels, yielding a feeling more like awe or respect (negative pleasure). Thus the wide stormy ocean may appear horrible unless the mind is already filled with Ideas enabling a sublime response.
